Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, quick roll call. I'm Maya from Redwood, daniel is here from SE.
[00:08] Daniel: hi all, hey, hey.
[00:10] Lena: Lena here, hi.
[00:12] Marcus: Marcus, infra.
[00:14] Priya: Priya, product.
[00:16] Maya: great, let's pick up where we left off last week. short agenda: econ recap, caching results, batching tradeoffs, then action items. does that work?
[00:28] Lena: yep fine. we sent over new request mix overnight, a lot more short prompts and some multi-turn chat.
[00:33] Daniel: saw that, thank you. i ran the initial throughput calc against the 7b-int8 variant and the int4 quantized variant. the high level: you currently sitting at ~4.1 tokens per dollar on hosted baseline with no cache, for the chat route. with prefix caching enabled we see about 22-28% token saving depending on prompt reuse.
[00:56] Marcus: wait 4.1 tokens per dollar, is that tokens per dollar or tokens/sec per dollar?
[01:02] Daniel: ah sorry bad shorthand — that's tokens per dollar. for the tokens/sec/$ metric, which you asked to prioritize, the 7b-int8 gives roughly 0.9 tokens/sec/$ under your median sequence length 120. int4 bumps that to about 1.5 tokens/sec/$ but there's a latency hit on tail percentiles.
[01:20] Priya: can you explain the latency-tails? we care about 95th p95 < 300ms for the UI otherwise the chat feels laggy.
[01:26] Daniel: sure. int4 quantization reduces cost but increases decode CPU work in our runtime path sometimes — you'll see more variance on p90/p95. with batch size 1 you get best latency but worst tokens/sec/$, with continuous batching size ~8 you improve tokens/sec/$ by around 25-35% but p95 can move from 280ms to 420ms depending on KV cache hit.
[01:48] Lena: so batching helps our dollars, but hurts the UI. is there a middle ground?
[01:52] Daniel: yes, adaptive batching + dynamic routing. our recommended config for VerdantAI's UI route is: batch ceiling 4, max wait 30ms, fallback to single-shot for priority sessions. that keeps p95 around 320ms but gets you ~18% improvement in tokens/sec/$.
[02:08] Maya: quick note: those numbers are from our pilot cluster where we used a mix of dedicated and hosted nodes. when you move to private or on-prem there are differences - Marcus you'll want to run the staging burst to confirm.
[02:19] Marcus: understood. question: you mentioned KV cache - what's the delta between prefix cache and KV cache in practice?
[02:24] Daniel: good question. prefix cache catches repeated beginnings of prompts — saves full token regen when reuse is high. KV cache (we sometimes call it token-state cache) helps multi-turn chat where past key/value pairs are reused — in our tests for your workload KV cache added another 10-12% saving on top of prefix cache. together typical savings hit 30-35% on the conversational routes we saw.
[02:46] Priya: our product team is worried about context freshness — if we cache too aggressively user-specific context could be stale. any guardrails?
[02:52] Daniel: yes, cache TTLs and per-session invalidation. we can scope cache keys by user id and conversation version. also we recommend short TTL for user data, longer TTL for static system prompts.
[03:04] Lena: latency numbers earlier seemed optimistic. were you testing with 1k concurrency or 100?
[03:08] Daniel: these are medium-load numbers — roughly 250 concurrent streams. during the 2-hour burst we want Marcus to try 600-800 concurrent to see how autoscaling triggers and how tokens/sec/$ behaves once we get queueing.
[03:20] Marcus: on autoscaling — if we run in our VPC with your private control plane, how's the SLA & scaling policy different from hosted?
[03:27] Maya: Dedicated pools have reserved capacity and predictable throughput; private deployments depend on the infra you provision — our control plane will manage the model variant and routing but the underlying GPU autoscale is your responsibility. we can provide recommended instance types and a scaling policy template.
[03:40] Marcus: please send those templates.
[03:42] Maya: will do.
[03:44] Daniel: back to econ: one thing we flagged — asynchronous embedding routes (the batch embedding job you sent) look much better with quantized models and larger batching. for embeddings we saw tokens/sec/$ equivalent improvements of 3-4x when moving from batch size 1 to batch size 128 on dedicated infra. that's less sensitive to p95 because embeddings are async.
[04:05] Priya: interesting, so we should batch embeddings but keep chat mostly low-batch.
[04:09] Daniel: exactly. split routes by SLAs. chat: low-latency config, embeddings & indexing: high-batch quantized config.
[04:16] Lena: you mentioned model variants — could we toggle int4 only for background jobs and stick with int8 for user-facing chat?
[04:20] Daniel: yes, smart routing can send user-facing calls to int8 instances and background to int4. tradeoff is operational complexity and slightly higher cost with two pools. but it's common.
[04:30] Marcus: security question: we need SOC2 and audit log coverage in the private deployment. do you support encrypted audit logs and KMS integration?
[04:36] Maya: yes, private supports KMS/HSM integrations, encrypted at rest, and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. we'll attach our SOC2 docs in the follow-up.
[04:45] Priya: also SSO — SAML side?
[04:47] Maya: SSO and SAML are supported for console access. we'll include setup steps.
[04:52] Lena: coming back to cost — what realistic tokens-per-dollar target should we set in our success criteria? our CFO wants a conservative projection.
[04:58] Daniel: conservative: target ~3 tokens/$ for user chat assuming minimal cache, optimistic: 6-7 tokens/$ with prefix+KV caching and adaptive batching. but tokens/sec/$ metric for throughput economics: conservative 0.8 tokens/sec/$, optimistic 2.0 tokens/sec/$. i'll put both conservative and optimistic into the spreadsheet.
[05:18] Marcus: those optimistic numbers assume dedicated GPUs?
[05:21] Daniel: yes, dedicated + burst capacity. hosted can approach optimistic if you use our higher-tier instance classes, but dedicated tends to be more predictable.
[05:28] Priya: ok agreed, let's put conservative in the contract and aim to prove upsides in the pilot.
[05:32] Maya: sounds good. action items recap in a sec.
[05:36] Daniel: quick note on instrumentation — we've added token-level traces and route-level cost counters to the console. we've also attached a small script (link shared in chat) that Marcus can drop into staging to forward per-call latency and token counts to our dashboard.
[05:49] Marcus: i saw the slack link; i'll try to wire it up after lunch.
[05:52] Lena: any red flags we should watch for in the 2-hr burst?
[05:55] Daniel: yes: monitor tail latency spikes (p95/p99), queue depth (if autoscaler isn't fast enough you see big dips in tokens/sec/$), and error rates for the int4 variants — occasionally you see a small increase in generation anomalies with aggressive quant.
[06:09] Priya: generation anomalies how bad? gibberish?
[06:11] Daniel: usually hallucination rate increases slightly on rare prefixes; we'll run regression tests with your prompt set. if we observe issues we can fallback to int8 per-route.
[06:20] Lena: can you include the regen/fallback policy example in the doc?
[06:23] Daniel: yes, will include a YAML snippet showing canary rollout + automatic fallback when quality regression crosses threshold.
[06:28] Maya: ok, time to summarize next steps. Daniel to share updated econ spreadsheet with per-route rows, int8/int4 cost columns, caching assumptions, and tokens/sec/$ calcs by 2026-09-10. Marcus to run the 2-hour burst with caching toggled on/off and send logs by 2026-09-12. Priya to finalize and share success criteria doc by 2026-09-11. Maya to send pilot pricing and extension options by 2026-09-09.
[06:54] Marcus: quick question on billing — if we exceed pilot reserved capacity during burst, what happens?
[06:58] Maya: you'll get billed at overage rates for hosted; for dedicated pilot we can set a soft cap and notify before auto-scale beyond commit. we'll put the exact numbers in the pricing doc.
[07:08] Lena: great. one more small ask: can we get a sample traffic shaping policy for activating priority sessions for internal agents?
[07:15] Daniel: yes, sample policy and a short script to map priority headers -> queue.
[07:20] Priya: thanks.
[07:22] Speaker 1: (inaudible)

[07:33] Lena: thanks all.
